chem_ocra.5.0.summary: Mastering chemical formulae for elements, compounds, and ions is the fundamental language of OCR GCSE Chemistry. To achieve a grade 9, you must know the exact valencies, charges, and atomic symbols for standard elements, common covalent molecules, and crucial polyatomic ions. This enables you to construct balanced formulae using the crossover method and interpret formulas accurately in equations.

core.p: Every element on the Periodic Table has a unique one- or two-letter chemical symbol. The first letter is always uppercase, and the second letter is always lowercase.
bullets: Single-letter symbols include Hydrogen (H), Carbon (C), Nitrogen (N), and Oxygen (O).
Two-letter symbols include Sodium (Na), Chlorine (Cl), Calcium (Ca), and Iron (Fe).
Symbols represent single atoms of an element when written on their own.
Some elements exist as single atoms (monatomic), such as the noble gases (He, Ne, Ar).

callouts.p: Always write the second letter of a chemical symbol in lowercase. Writing CO for Cobalt means something completely different from Co, which is Carbon Monoxide.

core.p: Certain non-metal elements do not exist as single atoms under normal conditions. Instead, they form covalent molecules consisting of two atoms bonded together.
bullets: The seven key diatomic elements are Hydrogen (H2), Nitrogen (N2), Oxygen (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2).
Remember the mnemonic: Have No Fear Of Ice Cold Beer (H, N, F, O, I, Cl, Br).
Halogens and other diatomic gases must always be written with a subscript 2 when referring to the element as a standalone substance in chemical equations.
Ozone exists as triatomic oxygen (O3), but normal atmospheric oxygen is diatomic (O2).

callouts.p: Never write 2H for hydrogen gas; 2H means two separate hydrogen atoms, whereas H2 means one molecule containing two bonded hydrogen atoms.

fig.cap: Visual representation of a diatomic oxygen molecule (O2) showing two oxygen atoms covalently bonded with a double bond.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><circle cx="150" cy="120" r="50" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="250" cy="120" r="50" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="3"/><text x="150" y="125" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">O</text><text x="250" y="125" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">O</text><text x="200" y="60" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Covalent bond in O₂</text></svg>

core.p: Compounds are formed when two or more different elements are chemically bonded together in fixed proportions. Their chemical formulae show the exact ratio of atoms.
bullets: Water is represented as H2O, showing two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom.
Carbon dioxide is CO2, showing one carbon atom for every two oxygen atoms.
Subscript numbers apply only to the atom immediately preceding them unless brackets are used.
Compounds can be composed of simple molecules or giant lattice structures.

callouts.p: A combination of symbols showing the elements present in a compound and their relative proportions.

core.p: Ions are atoms or groups of atoms that have lost or gained electrons, resulting in a full outer shell and a net electrical charge.
bullets: Metal atoms lose electrons to form positively charged ions called cations.
Non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negatively charged ions called anions.
The magnitude of the charge corresponds to the number of electrons lost or gained.
Group 1 metals form +1 ions, Group 2 form +2 ions, and Group 3 form +3 ions.

callouts.p: Group 7 elements form -1 ions (halides), Group 6 form -2 ions, and Group 5 form -3 ions.

core.p: Polyatomic ions are groups of covalently bonded atoms that carry an overall electrical charge. You must learn their names, formulae, and charges by heart.
bullets: Hydroxide ion: OH⁻ (charge -1)
Nitrate ion: NO₃⁻ (charge -1)
Sulfate ion: SO₄²⁻ (charge -2)
Carbonate ion: CO₃²⁻ (charge -2)
Ammonium ion: NH₄⁺ (charge +1 - the only common positive polyatomic ion)

callouts.p: Always use brackets around a polyatomic ion when you need more than one of them in a formula, e.g., Calcium hydroxide is Ca(OH)₂.

core.p: Transition metals can form ions with different positive charges. Roman numerals in IUPAC nomenclature indicate the exact charge on the metal ion.
bullets: Iron(II) contains the Fe²⁺ ion.
Iron(III) contains the Fe³⁺ ion.
Copper(I) contains Cu⁺ and Copper(II) contains Cu²⁺.
Silver is typically written as Ag⁺ and Zinc as Zn²⁺ (these do not use Roman numerals as they only form one ion type).

callouts.p: The Roman numeral represents the charge of the metal ion, not the number of atoms of that metal in the formula.

core.h: 7. The Crossover Method for Ionic Formulae
core.p: To deduce the chemical formula of an ionic compound, the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge so the compound is neutral overall.
bullets: Step 1: Write down the symbols and charges of the two ions.
Step 2: Cross the numbers of the charges down to become the subscript for the opposite ion.
Step 3: Simplify the ratio of subscripts if possible (e.g., Mg2O2 becomes MgO).
Step 4: Remove the charge signs and omit the number 1 if applicable.

callouts.p: Ionic compounds have zero overall charge. The positive charges balance the negative charges completely.

fig.cap: Step-by-step visual guide for the crossover method using Magnesium and Chloride ions to form MgCl2.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="40" y="40" width="120" height="60" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1e40af" rx="8"/><text x="100" y="75" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Mg²⁺   Cl⁻</text><path d="M 100 110 L 100 140" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="200" y="125" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Crossover</text><rect x="240" y="150" width="120" height="60" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#15803d" rx="8"/><text x="300" y="185" font-size="18" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">MgCl₂</text></svg>

core.p: When a formula requires multiple polyatomic ions, brackets must enclose the entire ion formula, with the multiplier placed outside as a subscript.
bullets: Example: Aluminium sulfate. Ions are Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
Cross the charges: Al gets a 2, SO₄ gets a 3.
Write with brackets: Al₂(SO₄)₃.
This indicates two aluminium ions for every three sulfate ions.

callouts.p: Writing Al2SO43 without brackets is completely incorrect because it changes the meaning of the oxygen and sulfur counts.

core.p: State symbols are added to chemical equations in parentheses after each formula to show the physical state of each substance under the reaction conditions.
bullets: (s) stands for solid.
(l) stands for liquid (pure liquid, not a solution).
(g) stands for gas.
(aq) stands for aqueous, meaning dissolved in water (an aqueous solution).

callouts.p: Hydrochloric acid is always written as HCl(aq) because it is a solution of hydrogen chloride gas dissolved in water.

core.p: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
bullets: For covalent molecules like glucose (C6H12O6), the empirical formula is CH2O.
Ionic compounds always have formulae that represent their empirical formula because giant lattices do not consist of discrete molecules.
Calculated from mass or percentage composition data by finding moles of atoms and simplifying the ratio.

callouts.p: The simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.

analogy.t: Chemical Formulae as Alphabet and Recipe Words
analogy.p: Think of chemical symbols as letters of an alphabet, and chemical formulae as words. Individual atoms are single letters, diatomic elements are double letters that always travel in pairs (like 'LL' or 'OO'), and ionic compounds are words formed by balancing positive and negative puzzle pieces. Where the analogy breaks down is that chemical bonding involves exact electrical charges and energy states, whereas letters are combined purely by linguistic convention.

terms.d: A substance made of only one type of atom.
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded together.
A collection of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds.
An atom or group of atoms with an electrical charge due to loss or gain of electrons.
A positively charged ion formed by losing electrons.
A negatively charged ion formed by gaining electrons.
An ion containing more than one atom covalently bonded with an overall charge.
A shorthand method of representing the atoms and elements in a substance using symbols.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
Symbols (s, l, g, aq) used in equations to show the physical state of substances.
Consisting of two atoms joined by a covalent bond in each molecule.
Dissolved in water to form a solution.

mistakes.w: Writing H for hydrogen gas in equations
mistakes.r: Hydrogen is diatomic, so it must always be written as H2.

mistakes.w: Writing Mg2O2 for magnesium oxide
mistakes.r: Ionic formulae must be simplified to their simplest ratio, which is MgO.

mistakes.w: Forgetting brackets around polyatomic ions when multiplying
mistakes.r: Use brackets, e.g., Ca(OH)2, so the subscript applies to the whole ion.

mistakes.w: Writing uppercase for the second letter of an element symbol
mistakes.r: Cobalt is Co, not CO (which is carbon monoxide).

mistakes.w: Confusing transition metal Roman numerals with atom counts
mistakes.r: Roman numerals indicate the positive charge of the metal ion, e.g., Fe(III) means Fe3+.

mistakes.w: Using (l) for salt dissolved in water
mistakes.r: Substances dissolved in water must take the state symbol (aq), not (l).

mistakes.w: Writing 2Cl for chlorine gas molecules
mistakes.r: Chlorine gas is Cl2; 2Cl represents two separate chlorine atoms.

exam.q: State the chemical formula for water.
exam.tip: Ensure the 2 is written as a subscript.

exam.q: Give the formula for calcium nitrate.
exam.tip: Remember brackets around the nitrate ion since you need two of them.

exam.q: Explain why sodium chloride has the formula NaCl.
model: Sodium ion is Na+ and chloride ion is Cl-
Charges balance equally so the ratio is 1:1
exam.tip: Reference electrical neutrality and ion charges.

exam.q: Write the balanced formula for aluminium sulfate.
exam.tip: Cross the 3 and 2 charges down correctly.

exam.q: State the meaning of the state symbol (aq).
exam.tip: Do not just say liquid; must specify dissolved in water.

exam.q: Identify the diatomic element from this list: carbon, helium, oxygen, sulfur.
exam.tip: Recall Have No Fear Of Ice Cold Beer.

exam.q: Write the formula for iron(III) chloride.
exam.tip: Roman numeral III tells you the iron ion has a 3+ charge.

exam.q: What is the empirical formula of glucose, C6H12O6?
exam.tip: Divide all numbers by the highest common factor (6).

exam.q: Write the chemical formula for ammonium carbonate.
exam.tip: Ammonium is the positive polyatomic ion needing brackets here.

worked.q: Deduce the chemical formula of magnesium hydroxide given that magnesium is in Group 2 and the hydroxide ion is OH-.
steps: Identify the charge on the magnesium ion: Magnesium is in Group 2, so it forms a 2+ ion (Mg2+).
Identify the charge on the hydroxide ion: Hydroxide is a polyatomic ion with a 1- charge (OH-).
Apply the crossover method: Bring the 2 down to the hydroxide group and the 1 down to the magnesium.
Enclose the polyatomic ion in brackets since a multiplier greater than 1 is needed: Mg(OH)2.

worked.q: Find the empirical formula of a compound containing 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass.
steps: Write down the percentages: C = 85.7%, H = 14.3%.
Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass (Ar of C = 12, Ar of H = 1): C = 85.7 / 12 = 7.14, H = 14.3 / 1 = 14.3.
Divide both answers by the smallest number (7.14): C = 7.14 / 7.14 = 1, H = 14.3 / 7.14 = 2.
Write the empirical formula from the simplest whole-number ratio (1:2): CH2.

chem_ocra.5.2.summary: These comprehensive revision notes cover the OCR GCSE Chemistry specification point C3.1g-h on the mole, Avogadro constant, and relating mass to amount of substance. They explain how chemists use the mole as a counting unit for particles, define the Avogadro constant precisely, and guide students through mastering mass-moles calculations with step-by-step clarity. Designed for grade 9 mastery, every calculation rule, definition, and potential exam trap is meticulously broken down.

core.p: Atoms, molecules and ions are unimaginably tiny, meaning we can never count individual particles in a laboratory setting. Instead, chemists use a specialized unit called the mole to measure the amount of a substance.
bullets: A mole is simply a convenient counting unit used in chemistry.
One mole of any substance contains an exact number of particles.
The abbreviation for mole is 'mol'.
It bridges the gap between the submicroscopic world of atoms and the macroscopic world of weighable quantities in a laboratory.

callouts.p: The amount of a substance that contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles of that substance.

core.p: The number of particles in exactly one mole of any substance is a fundamental physical constant known as the Avogadro constant.
bullets: The value of the Avogadro constant is 6.02 x 10^23 per mole.
It applies to atoms, molecules, ions, or electrons.
One mole of carbon atoms contains 6.02 x 10^23 carbon atoms.
One mole of water molecules contains 6.02 x 10^23 water molecules, but 3 x 6.02 x 10^23 individual atoms.

callouts.p: Always use 6.02 x 10^23 in calculations unless the specific exam paper asks for a different rounded figure.

fig.cap: Diagram illustrating that one mole of different substances all contain the exact same number of particles (6.02 x 10^23), despite having vastly different masses.

core.h: Relative Atomic Mass and Molar Mass
core.p: Relative atomic mass (Ar) is the mean mass of an atom compared to 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Molar mass is simply this value expressed in grams per mole.
bullets: Relative atomic mass has no units because it is a ratio.
Molar mass has the unit grams per mole (g/mol).
For any single element, the molar mass is numerically equal to its relative atomic mass.
For compounds, sum the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the formula to find the relative formula mass (Mr).

callouts.p: Always write g/mol for molar mass in your working out to gain full communication marks.

core.h: Relating Mass to Amount of Substance
core.p: The core mathematical link between the mass of a sample in grams, its molar mass, and its amount in moles is given by a simple formula triangle.
bullets: Mass equals moles multiplied by molar mass.
Moles equals mass divided by molar mass.
Molar mass equals mass divided by moles.
Ensuring units match (grams and g/mol) is vital for accurate calculations.

callouts.p: The quantity of a chemical measured in moles, calculated using mass divided by molar mass.

fig.cap: Formula triangle showing the mathematical relationship between mass, moles, and molar mass.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><polygon points="200,30 320,190 80,190" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="115" x2="320" y2="115" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="115" x2="200" y2="190" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="85" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Mass (g)</text><text x="140" y="160" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Moles (mol)</text><text x="260" y="160" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Mr (g/mol)</text></svg>

core.p: To find out how many moles are present in a given mass of a substance, divide the given mass by the molar mass.
bullets: Step 1: Identify the chemical formula of the substance.
Step 2: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) from the periodic table.
Step 3: Divide the mass in grams by the calculated Mr.
Step 4: State your final answer with appropriate significant figures and units (mol).

callouts.p: Never divide molar mass by mass. Always divide mass by molar mass (Moles = Mass / Mr).

core.p: If you know the number of moles required for a chemical reaction, you can calculate the exact mass in grams to weigh out on a balance.
bullets: Step 1: Identify the required moles and chemical formula.
Step 2: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of the substance.
Step 3: Multiply the number of moles by the Mr.
Step 4: State the mass in grams (g).

callouts.p: In practical chemistry, we cannot measure moles directly; we must calculate the mass to use a digital balance.

core.p: Higher tier students must be able to convert between the amount in moles and the actual number of atoms, molecules, or ions using the Avogadro constant.
bullets: Number of particles equals moles multiplied by the Avogadro constant.
Moles equals number of particles divided by the Avogadro constant.
To find total atoms in a compound molecule, multiply the number of molecules by the total atoms per formula unit.

callouts.p: Number of particles = Moles x 6.02 x 10^23.

core.p: Examiners heavily penalize sloppy rounding in mole calculations. Maintain intermediate accuracy and round only at the final step.
bullets: Keep at least 3 significant figures in your working steps.
Match your final answer to the lowest number of significant figures given in the question data.
Do not round intermediate calculator displays prematurely.

callouts.p: Store intermediate calculation values in your calculator memory rather than writing and retyping rounded numbers.

core.p: Higher tier exam questions often combine mass-to-mole conversions with particle counts or percentage composition tasks in multi-mark scenarios.
bullets: Break complex questions down into distinct sequential steps.
Check if you need to find Mr before calculating moles.
Ensure all unit conversions (e.g., kg to g) are completed before applying formulas.

callouts.p: If a mass is given in kilograms, you must multiply by 1000 to convert to grams before dividing by molar mass.

fig.cap: Flowchart representing the conversion pathways between mass, moles, and number of particles.

core.h: Practical Applications in Titrations and Reacting Masses
core.p: Understanding moles allows chemists to predict exactly how much product will form in industrial processes and analytical titrations.
bullets: Reacting mass calculations rely entirely on mole ratios from balanced equations.
The mole acts as the universal exchange currency in chemical stoichiometry.
Experimental yields are compared with theoretical mole calculations to find percentage yield.

callouts.p: Coefficients in balanced equations represent the ratio of moles reacting, not the ratio of grams.

analogy.t: The Baker's Dozen and Gross Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine eggs being sold by the gross (144 eggs) rather than individually because they are too numerous and small to count one by one. In chemistry, the mole is simply our 'super-gross' containing 6.02 x 10^23 items. Just as a baker knows the mass of a dozen eggs depends on their size, a chemist knows the mass of a mole of atoms depends on the element's atomic weight. Where this analogy breaks down is that eggs in a dozen are all identical in mass, whereas in chemistry, one mole of lead is vastly heavier than one mole of carbon because lead atoms themselves contain far more protons and neutrons.

terms.d: The amount of substance that contains 6.02 x 10^23 specified particles.

terms.p: The number of atoms, molecules, or ions in one mole of a substance, equal to 6.02 x 10^23 per mole.
terms.d: The number of particles per mole of substance, 6.02 x 10^23.
The mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol).
The weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared to 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula of a compound.
A physical quantity measured in moles, representing the number of elementary entities.
The relationship between the relative quantities of substances taking part in a reaction.
Digits in a number that carry reliable information contributing to its precision.
A measure of the amount of matter in an object, usually measured in grams in chemistry calculations.
A general term for a subatomic particle, atom, molecule, or ion.
The number placed in front of a chemical formula in a balanced equation to represent moles.
A metric unit of mass equal to one thousandth of a kilogram.

mistakes.w: Saying a mole is a mass in grams.
mistakes.r: A mole is an amount of substance / number of particles, not a mass.

mistakes.w: Using the Avogadro constant as the unit for molar mass.
mistakes.r: Avogadro constant has units per mole (mol^-1); molar mass has units g/mol.

mistakes.w: Multiplying mass by Mr to find moles.
mistakes.r: Always divide mass by Mr to find moles (Moles = Mass / Mr).

mistakes.w: Forgetting that diatomic elements (O2, Cl2) have double the atomic mass.
mistakes.r: Use 32 g/mol for oxygen gas (O2), not 16 g/mol.

mistakes.w: Rounding numbers in the middle of a multi-step calculation.
mistakes.r: Keep full calculator display until the final answer step.

mistakes.w: Writing units as 'grams' instead of 'g' or 'g/mol'.
mistakes.r: Use standard accepted scientific symbols and units in exams.

mistakes.w: Confusing relative atomic mass with mass number.
mistakes.r: Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of isotopes; mass number is a whole integer for a single isotope.

exam.q: Define the term 'mole' in chemistry.
exam.tip: Mention both the concept of amount and the specific numerical value for full marks.

exam.q: Calculate the molar mass of magnesium chloride, MgCl2. (Ar: Mg = 24, Cl = 35.5)
exam.tip: Show your addition clearly and include units.

exam.q: Calculate the number of moles in 22 g of carbon dioxide, CO2. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16)
exam.tip: Always state the Mr calculation first before dividing.

exam.q: Calculate the mass of 0.25 moles of calcium carbonate, CaCO3. (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
exam.tip: Check your addition for the Mr carefully.

exam.q: Calculate the number of water molecules in 0.5 moles of water, H2O. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 x 10^23)
model: Number = Moles x Avogadro constant = 0.5 x 6.02 x 10^23 (1)
exam.tip: Show standard index form correctly.

exam.q: Explain why one mole of iron and one mole of carbon have different masses.
model: Iron atoms have a greater relative atomic mass than carbon atoms (1)
because iron nuclei contain more protons and neutrons (1)
exam.tip: Link mass difference to subatomic particle composition.

exam.q: A student burns 4.8 g of magnesium. Calculate the number of magnesium atoms reacted. (Ar: Mg = 24, L = 6.02 x 10^23)
model: Number of atoms = Moles x Avogadro constant (1)
exam.tip: Break multi-step calculations into distinct mole and particle stages.

exam.q: State the value of the Avogadro constant.
exam.tip: Memorize this exact figure.

exam.q: Calculate the mass of 3.01 x 10^23 molecules of sulfur dioxide, SO2. (Ar: S = 32, O = 16, L = 6.02 x 10^23)
model: Moles = Particles / Avogadro constant = 3.01 x 10^23 / 6.02 x 10^23 = 0.5 mol (1)
exam.tip: Convert particles to moles first before finding mass.

exam.q: A sample of gas contains 0.05 moles. What is its mass if the molar mass is 32 g/mol?
exam.tip: Double check decimal placement in multiplication.

worked.q: Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in a 40 g sample. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
steps: Step 1: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of NaOH. Mr = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40.
Step 2: Use the moles formula: Moles = Mass / Mr.
Step 3: Substitute values: Moles = 40 / 40 = 1.0 mol.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of 0.4 moles of copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4. (Ar: Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16)
steps: Step 1: Calculate the relative formula mass of CuSO4. Mr = 63.5 + 32 + (4 x 16) = 159.5.
Step 2: Use the mass formula: Mass = Moles x Mr.
Step 3: Substitute values: Mass = 0.4 x 159.5 = 63.8 g.

worked.q: Calculate the number of oxygen atoms in 0.2 moles of carbon dioxide (CO2). (Avogadro constant = 6.02 x 10^23)
steps: Step 1: Find the number of CO2 molecules by multiplying moles by the Avogadro constant: 0.2 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.204 x 10^23 molecules.
Step 2: Note that each CO2 molecule contains 2 oxygen atoms.
Step 3: Multiply molecules by 2: 1.204 x 10^23 x 2 = 2.408 x 10^23 oxygen atoms.

chem_ocra.5.1.summary: Mastering chemical equations is fundamental for top-tier success in OCR GCSE Chemistry. This comprehensive guide covers balancing standard chemical equations, constructing ionic equations by eliminating spectator ions, writing half equations for oxidation and reduction, and accurately applying state symbols. Every section is designed to bridge the gap between basic reactions and grade 9 analytical chemistry.

core.p: Chemical equations represent chemical reactions using symbols and formulae. They show how reactants are converted into products, obeying the law of conservation of mass where atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
bullets: Left-hand side contains reactants separated by plus signs.
Right-hand side contains products separated by plus signs.
An arrow pointing right indicates the direction of the chemical change.
Every valid equation must be quantitatively balanced.

callouts.p: A representation of a chemical reaction using the chemical formulae of the reactants and products.
Never alter the small subscript numbers inside a chemical formula to balance an equation; only change the large coefficients in front.

core.p: Balancing equations ensures that the total number of atoms of each element is identical on both sides. We achieve this by placing whole numbers, called stoichiometric coefficients, in front of the chemical formulae.
bullets: Count the number of atoms of each element on the reactant and product sides.
Balance elements one at a time, leaving hydrogen and oxygen until the end.
Check polyatomic ions (like SO4 2-) as single units if they remain unchanged.
Multiply coefficients across entire formulae.

callouts.p: The number of atoms of each element must balance across the reaction arrow.
Balancing complex molecules becomes much easier if you balance hydrogen and oxygen atoms last.

fig.cap: Visual representation of balancing hydrogen reacting with oxygen to form water, showing atom counts before and after balancing.

core.p: State symbols provide vital physical information about the state of matter of each reactant and product under reaction conditions. They are written in parentheses immediately after each chemical formula.
bullets: (s) represents a solid substance.
(l) represents a pure liquid substance.
(aq) represents an aqueous solution dissolved in water.
(g) represents a gaseous substance.

callouts.p: Abbreviations used in chemical equations to indicate the physical state of reactants and products.

core.p: When ionic compounds react in aqueous solution, many ions do not participate directly in the chemical change. Ionic equations strip away these spectator ions to focus strictly on the chemical species undergoing change.
bullets: Write out the balanced full equation with state symbols.
Split all aqueous ionic substances into their respective constituent ions.
Identify and cancel out spectator ions appearing identically on both sides.
Rewrite the remaining species as the net ionic equation.

callouts.p: Ions that are present in a reaction mixture but do not take part in the chemical reaction itself.

core.p: Neutralisation reactions between strong acids and soluble bases always follow the same core ionic pathway. Hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce neutral water molecules.
bullets: Acids release hydrogen ions (H+) in aqueous solution.
Alkalis release hydroxide ions (OH-) in aqueous solution.
The core ionic equation is H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l).
Spectator ions like Na+ and Cl- are omitted from the net ionic equation.

callouts.p: All strong acid-alkali neutralisations simplify to H+ + OH- -> H2O.

core.p: Acids reacting with metal carbonates produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas. The ionic equation highlights the reaction of hydrogen ions with solid carbonate or dissolved carbonate species.
bullets: Carbonate ions are represented as CO3 2-.
Solid metal carbonates react via 2H+(aq) + CaCO3(s) -> Ca2+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g).
Carbon dioxide gas escapes, driving the reaction to completion.
State symbols are crucial here to show the dissolution and gas evolution.

callouts.p: Remember that most metal carbonates are insoluble (s), except Group 1 carbonates and ammonium carbonate.

core.p: Half equations model electron transfer processes during redox reactions. They show either oxidation (loss of electrons) or reduction (gain of electrons) separately for a specific chemical species.
bullets: Electrons are denoted by the symbol e-.
Oxidation half equations have electrons on the product side (loss).
Reduction half equations have electrons on the reactant side (gain).
Crucial for electrolysis and metal displacement reactions.

callouts.p: An equation that describes reduction or oxidation by showing the loss or gain of electrons.

core.p: During electrolysis, ions migrate to oppositely charged electrodes where they are discharged by gaining or losing electrons. Half equations allow us to track these electrode processes precisely.
bullets: At the cathode (negative electrode), positive ions gain electrons (reduction).
At the anode (positive electrode), negative ions lose electrons (oxidation).
Example for copper ions: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.
Example for chloride ions: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-.

callouts.p: Never place electrons on the wrong side of the arrow; remember OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons).

fig.cap: Diagram showing electron transfer at electrodes during electrolysis, illustrating reduction at cathode and oxidation at anode.

core.h: Combining Half Equations into Redox Equations
core.p: Overall redox equations can be derived by combining reduction and oxidation half equations. The number of electrons lost in oxidation must equal the number of electrons gained in reduction.
bullets: Write down the oxidation and reduction half equations.
Multiply one or both equations so electron numbers match.
Add the two half equations together and cancel out the electrons.
Verify that atoms and charges balance on both sides.

callouts.p: The electrons lost must exactly equal the electrons gained in any combined redox equation.

core.p: Metal displacement reactions involve a more reactive metal displacing a less reactive metal ion from solution. Writing these as ionic equations highlights the actual electron transfer taking place.
bullets: Full equation: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s).
Ionic equation: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) -> Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s).
Spectator sulfate ions (SO4 2-) are removed.
Zinc is oxidised (loses electrons), while copper ions are reduced (gain electrons).

callouts.p: A reaction where a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.

core.p: Examiners frequently penalize students for common sloppy habits when writing equations. Attention to detail regarding state symbols, ion charges, and balancing coefficients is essential.
bullets: Failing to include state symbols when specifically requested by command words.
Writing incorrect ionic charges (e.g., writing Cl instead of Cl-).
Leaving equations unbalanced in terms of charge or atom count.
Forgetting diatomic molecules like Cl2, O2, and H2.

callouts.p: Never write oxygen as O in an equation; it is always O2 (similarly for H2, N2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2).

analogy.p: Balancing equations is like following a recipe where ingredients (reactants) must combine in precise ratios to bake cakes (products), and you cannot magically create or destroy ingredients. Ionic equations are like filtering out the kitchen utensils that were present during baking but didn't end up inside the final cake.

terms.d: An equation for a chemical reaction in which the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.
Letters written in brackets after each formula in a chemical equation to indicate physical state: (s), (l), (g), (aq).
An equation for reactions in aqueous solution showing only the reacting ions, omitting spectator ions.
An ion that does not change its chemical state or take part during a chemical reaction.
An equation showing either oxidation or reduction, explicitly including electrons.
Loss of electrons or gain of oxygen during a chemical reaction.
Gain of electrons or loss of oxygen during a chemical reaction.
Describing a substance dissolved in water, denoted by (aq).
An insoluble solid formed by the reaction of two aqueous solutions.
The reaction between acid and base producing salt and water, ionic core H+ + OH- -> H2O.
The numerical relationship between relative quantities of reactants and products in a balanced equation.
A large number placed in front of a chemical formula to indicate how many units take part.

mistakes.w: Changing the formula subscript to balance an equation
mistakes.r: Only change large front coefficients; changing subscripts changes the chemical identity.

mistakes.w: Omitting state symbols when not explicitly prompted
mistakes.r: Always include state symbols if the question asks for a full equation with state symbols.

mistakes.w: Including spectator ions in an ionic equation
mistakes.r: Cancel out ions that appear unchanged on both sides before writing the net ionic equation.

mistakes.w: Writing oxygen as O instead of O2
mistakes.r: Gases like oxygen, hydrogen, and chlorine are diatomic molecules (O2, H2, Cl2).

mistakes.w: Writing incorrect ionic charges like Na2+
mistakes.r: Sodium is in Group 1, so its ion is always Na+.

mistakes.w: Placing electrons on the wrong side of a half equation
mistakes.r: Remember OIL RIG: electrons are products in oxidation, reactants in reduction.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to balance total electrical charge in ionic equations
mistakes.r: The sum of ionic charges on the reactant side must equal the sum on the product side.

exam.q: Balance the following equation: Fe + HCl -> FeCl3 + H2
exam.tip: Balance chlorine and hydrogen last since iron is alone initially.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide solution.
exam.tip: Remember spectator ions Na+ and Cl- are removed.

exam.q: Explain what the state symbol (aq) means.
exam.tip: Keep it brief and exact for 1 mark.

exam.q: Write a balanced half equation for the reduction of copper(II) ions to copper metal.
model: Correct species and electrons on correct side
exam.tip: Reduction means gain of electrons, so electrons go on the left.

exam.q: A solution of silver nitrate is mixed with sodium chloride solution, forming a white precipitate of silver chloride. Write the ionic equation with state symbols.
exam.tip: Precipitates are solids (s) formed from aqueous solutions.

exam.q: Describe the mistake in the following student equation for burning magnesium: Mg + O -> MgO
model: Oxygen is written as an single atom O instead of diatomic O2
Equation is not balanced (should be 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO)
exam.tip: Always check for diatomic elements when elements react alone.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of dilute hydrochloric acid with calcium carbonate.
model: Correct state symbols including (s) for carbonate
exam.tip: Solid carbonates do not split into ions in ionic equations.

exam.q: Explain why spectator ions are omitted from net ionic equations.
model: They do not take part in the chemical reaction
They remain unchanged on both sides of the equation
exam.tip: Mention non-participation and unchanged state.

exam.q: Construct a balanced redox equation from the half equations: Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e- and Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-
exam.tip: Ensure electrons on left and right match before adding.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the combustion of methane (CH4) in oxygen, including state symbols.
exam.tip: Combustion produces carbon dioxide and water vapor or liquid water.

worked.q: Construct the balanced ionic equation for the reaction between aqueous zinc sulfate and barium chloride, noting that barium sulfate is an insoluble precipitate.
steps: Step 1: Write the full balanced equation with state symbols: ZnSO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + BaSO4(s)
Step 2: Split all aqueous ionic compounds into ions: Zn2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) + Ba2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq) -> Zn2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq) + BaSO4(s)
Step 3: Identify and cancel spectator ions (Zn2+ and Cl-)
Step 4: Write remaining species as the net ionic equation.

worked.q: Balance the tricky equation for the combustion of ammonia: NH3 + O2 -> NO + H2O
steps: Step 1: Balance nitrogen and hydrogen first: 4NH3 + O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O
Step 2: Count oxygen atoms on the product side: (4 x 1) + (6 x 1) = 10 oxygen atoms.
Step 3: Place a coefficient of 5 in front of O2 on the reactant side to get 10 oxygen atoms (5 x 2 = 10).
Step 4: Double-check all atom counts: N=4, H=12, O=10 on both sides.
